analogy.p: A home thermostat switches the heating on when the room is too cold and the cooling on when it is too warm, keeping the temperature near a set value. Insulin is the cooling switch that brings blood glucose down after a meal, glucagon is the heating switch that pushes it up between meals, and the pancreas is the thermostat that senses the level. In type 1 diabetes the cooling switch is broken; in type 2 the radiators ignore the signal. The analogy breaks down because hormones travel in the blood to many organs rather than along a wire, and the body has no single fixed set point to dial.
analogy.t: A thermostat with a heating and cooling switch

bullets: Blood glucose is kept within a **narrow range** even though glucose intake varies hugely (big meal, fasting overnight, hard exercise).
Glucose comes from the **digestion of carbohydrates** (starch is broken down by amylase and carbohydrases to glucose), which is absorbed into the blood in the small intestine.
Glucose is used in **respiration** (aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, releasing energy), so exercise and growth lower blood glucose.
Control systems have three parts: **receptors** detect a change, a **coordination centre** processes the information, and **effectors** bring about the response that restores the optimum.
Both the nervous system and the **endocrine (hormonal) system** can coordinate responses; blood glucose control is hormonal.
If control fails the result is **diabetes**, a condition in which blood glucose concentration cannot be kept in the normal range.
core.h: Why blood glucose must be controlled (homeostasis)
core.p: **Homeostasis** is the regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function, in response to internal and external changes. Blood **glucose concentration** is one of the conditions the body controls, along with body temperature and water content. Glucose is the fuel for **respiration**, so every cell needs a steady supply. If blood glucose falls too low, brain cells in particular cannot release enough energy and the person becomes confused, faint or may lose consciousness. If it stays too high, water is drawn out of cells by osmosis and the kidneys cannot reabsorb all the glucose, so the person becomes dehydrated and the long-term damage of diabetes follows.

bullets: Endocrine glands secrete hormones **directly into the blood**; they have no ducts.
Hormones are chemicals (insulin and glucagon are **proteins**), carried in the **plasma** around the whole body but only affect cells with the matching receptors.
The **pancreas** is located just below the stomach and acts as the **monitor and controller** of blood glucose concentration.
Compared with nerves: hormones are **chemical**, travel in **blood**, give a **slower** response, with an effect that lasts **longer**.
Insulin and glucagon have **opposite effects**, so they are called **antagonistic hormones** (Higher tier idea, but useful at all levels).
The **liver** is the main target organ for both hormones; **muscle** and other body cells are also targets for insulin.
core.h: Hormones and the endocrine system: the basics
core.p: Blood glucose is controlled by **hormones**. A hormone is a chemical messenger secreted directly into the **bloodstream** by an **endocrine gland**. The blood carries the hormone to its **target organ**, where it binds to specific **receptors** and changes how the cells work. Because hormones travel in the blood, hormonal responses are generally **slower** than nervous responses but act for **longer** and can affect more than one organ. The two hormones that control glucose, **insulin** and **glucagon**, are made by the **pancreas**, which is both an endocrine gland and a digestive organ (it also makes digestive enzymes).

bullets: Step 1: carbohydrate is digested and glucose is absorbed, so **blood glucose rises**.
Step 2: the **pancreas detects** the high blood glucose concentration.
Step 3: the pancreas **secretes insulin** into the blood.
Step 4: insulin travels in the blood to the **liver, muscles and other cells** and makes them **take up glucose** from the blood.
Step 5: in the **liver (and muscles)** glucose is converted to **glycogen** for storage.
Step 6: **blood glucose falls** back to the normal level and insulin release reduces.
Exam phrase: insulin 'causes glucose to move from the blood into the cells' and 'converts glucose to glycogen in the liver'.
Do not say insulin 'turns into' anything or 'breaks down' glucose; it is a **signal**, not an enzyme.
core.h: What happens after a meal: the role of insulin
core.p: When you eat a meal containing carbohydrate, glucose is absorbed from the small intestine and blood glucose concentration **rises**. The **pancreas** detects this rise and responds by releasing the hormone **insulin** into the blood. Insulin is carried to the **liver** and other body cells (such as muscle). Insulin makes the cells take glucose **out of the blood** so the concentration falls. In the liver insulin also causes glucose to be converted into **glycogen** for storage. As blood glucose drops back toward normal, the pancreas releases less insulin, which is why the system settles at a steady value rather than overshooting.

bullets: Glycogen is a **polymer of glucose** (many glucose units joined in long, branched chains).
It is **insoluble**, so storing glucose as glycogen does not change the concentration of solutions inside cells.
Stored in the **liver** (a reserve for the whole body) and **muscle** cells (a local energy store).
**Insulin** → glucose to glycogen; **glucagon** → glycogen back to glucose.
Plants store glucose as **starch**; animals store it as **glycogen**; both are polysaccharides.
Stores are limited: if glycogen stores are full, excess glucose is converted into **fat** for long-term storage (a link to obesity and type 2 diabetes).
core.h: Glycogen: the storage form of glucose
core.p: **Glycogen** is a large, branched, insoluble carbohydrate made of many glucose molecules joined together. Because it is insoluble it does not affect the water balance of cells, so the body can store large amounts without disturbing osmosis. It is stored mainly in the **liver** and in the **muscles**. Liver glycogen can be broken down and released as glucose into the blood to supply the whole body, whereas muscle glycogen is used mainly by the muscle itself during exercise. Making glycogen from glucose is a **storage** process that is stimulated by insulin, while the reverse process is stimulated by glucagon.

bullets: Step 1: blood glucose **falls** (no food, exercise, growth).
Step 2: the **pancreas detects** the low glucose concentration.
Step 3: the pancreas **releases glucagon** into the blood.
Step 4: glucagon reaches the **liver**, where **glycogen is broken down to glucose**.
Step 5: glucose is **released into the blood**, so blood glucose rises back to normal.
Exercise: muscles use glucose faster, so blood glucose tends to fall; this is why diabetics may need less insulin or extra carbohydrate when exercising.
Glucagon and insulin are released **at different times** depending on whether blood glucose is above or below normal.
core.h: When blood glucose falls: the role of glucagon
core.p: Between meals, during fasting and during exercise, blood glucose concentration **falls** because cells keep using glucose in respiration. The **pancreas** detects the low concentration and releases the hormone **glucagon**. Glucagon travels in the blood to the **liver**, where it causes **glycogen to be converted back into glucose**. The glucose is released into the blood, so blood glucose concentration **rises** back to normal. This is why a healthy person does not run out of glucose overnight even though they have not eaten for hours.

bullets: **Negative feedback** = the response counteracts the original change (high glucose → insulin → glucose falls).
**Antagonistic** = two hormones with opposite effects controlling one condition.
High glucose → **insulin** → glucose to cells and glycogen → glucose **falls**.
Low glucose → **glucagon** → glycogen to glucose → glucose **rises**.
The pancreas is both the **receptor and coordination centre**; the **liver and muscle** are the effectors.
A good 4 mark answer names the hormone, its source, its target and the effect on blood glucose for BOTH directions.
Graph shape of a healthy person: small rise after eating then a return to the starting level within a couple of hours (a **fluctuation around a set point**).
Compare with body temperature control and water balance, which are also negative feedback systems.
core.h: Negative feedback and antagonistic hormones (Higher tier)
core.p: The control of blood glucose is an example of **negative feedback**: a change in a condition triggers a response that **reverses** the change and returns the condition to its normal level. Insulin and glucagon work **antagonistically** (in opposition): insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it. Together they interact so that blood glucose is held close to a **set point**. If glucose is too high the pancreas secretes insulin; if it is too low the pancreas secretes glucagon. Because each response removes the stimulus that caused it, the system is self-correcting and stable.

bullets: Cause: the pancreas **fails to produce sufficient insulin**.
Effect: blood glucose **cannot be lowered**, so it can rise to a **fatal** level after a meal.
Typical symptoms: **thirst**, frequent urination, tiredness, weight loss, glucose in the urine.
The kidney cannot reabsorb all the glucose when the blood concentration is very high, so some is **excreted in urine**.
Cells are normal and would respond to insulin; the problem is the **supply** of the hormone.
It is not caused by eating too much sugar, and it cannot be 'caught' from another person (it is not a communicable disease).
Diabetes is a **non-communicable disease** (link to risk factors in 4.2.2).
core.p: In **type 1 diabetes** the pancreas **does not produce enough insulin** (often it produces almost none) because the cells that make insulin have been destroyed. After a meal, blood glucose rises but nothing signals the liver and other cells to take it up, so blood glucose can rise to a **dangerously high level** and stay there. The person feels very thirsty, passes large amounts of urine (glucose is lost in the urine, drawing water with it), is tired and loses weight because cells cannot use the glucose. Without treatment it is fatal. It often appears in childhood or early adulthood and is not caused by lifestyle.

bullets: **Insulin injections** (often before meals) to lower blood glucose; insulin must be injected because digestive enzymes would break it down if taken orally.
**Carbohydrate-controlled diet** and regular meals so the insulin dose can be matched to intake.
**Monitoring** blood glucose concentration regularly (finger-prick test or continuous monitor).
Too much insulin (or not enough food) makes blood glucose fall too low (**hypoglycaemia**): confusion, sweating, faintness; treated with sugary food or drink.
Exercise lowers blood glucose, so dose and food may need adjusting.
Treatment is lifelong; it **controls but does not cure** the disease.
Insulin is now made by genetically modified bacteria (link to genetic engineering).
core.p: Type 1 diabetes is controlled by **insulin injections** and by managing **diet**. The insulin replaces the hormone the pancreas does not make, so after a meal it can lower blood glucose. The dose and timing must match carbohydrate intake and activity: a person usually injects before meals and monitors their blood glucose, and limits the amount of simple carbohydrate eaten at once. Insulin is given by injection (not as a tablet) because it is a **protein** and would be digested by protease enzymes in the stomach and small intestine if swallowed. The treatment controls the condition but does not cure it.

bullets: Cause: body cells **stop responding to insulin** (insulin resistance).
Blood glucose stays **high** after meals because uptake into cells and conversion to glycogen is reduced.
**Obesity** is a major risk factor; others include inactivity, poor diet, age and family history.
Often develops later in life and gradually, so may be undiagnosed for years.
Complications of long-term high glucose: damage to eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels (e.g. poor circulation in feet).
Rising obesity means type 2 diabetes is a growing **public health** problem with a large cost to the NHS.
core.h: Type 2 diabetes: cause and risk factors
core.p: In **type 2 diabetes** the body cells **no longer respond to insulin** (they have become **insulin resistant**), so even though insulin is present, glucose is not taken up properly and the blood glucose concentration stays too high. The pancreas may also produce too little insulin later. **Obesity** is a major risk factor because extra body fat is linked to insulin resistance. It is more common in older adults, those with a family history and people who are inactive, though it is increasingly seen in younger people as obesity rises. It is far more common than type 1 diabetes.

bullets: **Carbohydrate-controlled diet**, especially limiting sugary food and high glycaemic foods.
Regular **exercise** (muscles use glucose and become more sensitive to insulin).
**Weight loss** in obese patients can reduce or reverse the condition.
Medication may be prescribed if lifestyle changes are not enough.
Unlike type 1, injections are not always needed because the problem is **response**, not **supply**.
Prevention: healthy weight, balanced diet, exercise (link to the risk factors in non-communicable disease).
core.p: Type 2 diabetes is usually controlled first by **lifestyle changes**: a **carbohydrate-controlled diet**, increased **exercise** and **weight loss**. Exercise uses up glucose and improves how well cells respond to insulin, and losing weight reduces insulin resistance. In some patients, drugs that improve insulin response or increase insulin release, or eventually insulin injections, are also needed. Because it is linked to lifestyle, type 2 can often be **prevented or delayed** by maintaining a healthy body mass and staying active.

bullets: Type 1: **pancreas does not produce enough insulin**; Type 2: **cells no longer respond to insulin**.
Type 1: treated with **insulin injections** plus diet; Type 2: **diet, exercise, weight loss** (and sometimes drugs or insulin).
Type 1: usually starts in **childhood**/young adults; Type 2: usually **later in life** (linked to obesity).
Type 1 is **not preventable by lifestyle**; type 2 risk is **reduced** by healthy weight and exercise.
Both involve **high blood glucose** and glucose in the urine if untreated.
Type 2 is **much more common** than type 1.
core.p: Examination questions often ask you to compare the two types. The key difference is **where the problem lies**. In type 1 the pancreas does not make enough insulin (a problem of **supply**). In type 2 the cells do not respond properly to insulin (a problem of **response**). This explains the different treatments: type 1 must be treated with insulin injections, whereas type 2 is often managed with diet, exercise and weight loss. Both result in blood glucose that is too high after eating, and both require long-term management.

bullets: Describe the **trend first** (rises/falls), then give **numbers from the graph** with units.
Compare the **starting value**, the **peak value**, the **time to return** to normal.
Healthy: returns to the starting level; diabetic: stays high or falls slowly.
Percentage change = (change ÷ original value) × 100.
If a question says 'suggest why', link the shape to insulin: 'no/too little insulin so glucose is not taken up'.
Remember that a person treated with insulin will show a curve closer to the healthy pattern.
A flat or low line after exercise can be explained by glucose being used in respiration.
core.h: Interpreting data and graphs about blood glucose
core.p: A common exam task is to describe or interpret a graph or table of blood glucose concentration against time after a meal for a healthy person and a person with diabetes. In a **healthy** person the concentration rises a little after eating then quickly returns to its starting level. In a person with **diabetes** (untreated) the starting level is higher, rises much more, and takes far longer to fall, or does not fall. For calculations, use figures from the graph with units and show working for **percentage change**. Always quote data (with units, usually mmol per dm3) when asked to describe a pattern.

bullets: Respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; exercise lowers blood glucose.
Digestion: carbohydrases break starch to glucose, which raises blood glucose.
Genetic engineering: the human insulin gene inserted into bacteria produces insulin in large quantities.
Kidney: with very high blood glucose some glucose appears in urine (used in diagnosis).
Non-communicable disease: obesity is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes, which raises cardiovascular disease risk.
Water balance and temperature control are other negative feedback systems.
Public health: obesity levels, cost to the NHS and prevention strategies.
core.p: Blood glucose control links to many other parts of the course. It is a classic **negative feedback** example like temperature and water balance. It links to **enzymes and digestion** (carbohydrases produce glucose), **respiration** (glucose is the fuel), **diffusion and osmosis** (high glucose affects water movement), **non-communicable diseases** (obesity and diabetes are risk factors for cardiovascular disease), **genetic engineering** (bacteria make human insulin) and the **kidney** (glucose in urine). Using these links in extended answers earns the reasoning marks.

exam: 1 mark (state/name): 'Name the organ that monitors blood glucose' → pancreas. 'Name the hormone' → insulin or glucagon, linked to the direction.
2 mark (describe): give the sequence: glucose rises → pancreas releases insulin → glucose falls.
3 mark (explain): add the target and effect: insulin makes liver convert glucose to glycogen and cells take up glucose.
4 mark (compare type 1 and type 2): one statement of cause for each, then one difference in treatment, then one about prevention or onset. Use 'whereas'.
6 mark (extended): cover both directions (insulin and glucagon), use 'negative feedback', include the organs involved, then link to diabetes; order the answer logically.
Command words: 'describe' = say what happens; 'explain' = say why with a reason; 'compare' = similarities and differences; 'suggest' = apply knowledge to new data.
Graph questions: quote values with units, state the trend first, compare starting level, peak and time to return.
Calculate % change: (change ÷ original) × 100, show working and give the answer to the requested decimal places.
Always use the board terms: 'glucose concentration of the blood', 'converted to glycogen', 'negative feedback'.
Never write 'sugar' for glucose in a mark scheme answer; write glucose.
Insulin injections questions: the reason is that insulin is a protein digested if swallowed.
For 'why does a type 2 diabetic not need insulin injections?': because the pancreas still makes insulin but the cells do not respond, so diet and exercise improve response.

mistakes.r: Insulin is made by the pancreas.
mistakes.w: Insulin is made in the liver / stomach.

mistakes.r: Insulin makes cells take up glucose from the blood and the liver convert glucose to glycogen; it is a hormone, not an enzyme.
Glucagon makes the liver convert glycogen to glucose, which is released into the blood.
mistakes.w: Glucagon turns glycogen into insulin (or glucose into glycogen).

mistakes.r: In type 1 the pancreas does not produce enough insulin; in type 2 the cells do not respond to insulin.
Type 1 is caused by the pancreas not making insulin; obesity is a risk factor for type 2.
mistakes.w: Type 1 diabetes is caused by eating too much sugar.

mistakes.r: Insulin is a protein that would be digested, so it is injected.
mistakes.w: Insulin is taken as a tablet.

mistakes.r: Insulin injections control type 1 diabetes; they do not cure it.
Humans store glucose as glycogen (starch is the plant store).
mistakes.w: Glucose is stored as starch in humans.

mistakes.r: It is controlled by hormones (the endocrine system), released by the pancreas.
mistakes.w: Blood sugar is controlled by the nervous system.

mistakes.r: Negative feedback means the response reverses the change and returns the condition to normal.
mistakes.w: Negative feedback means a bad response.

summary: The spec asks you to explain how the pancreas, insulin and glucagon keep blood glucose concentration within a narrow range by negative feedback, and to explain and compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes and their treatments. It matters because it is a standard homeostasis example and a frequent 4 to 6 mark question that rewards precise terms.

terms.d: The regulation of the internal conditions of a cell or organism to maintain optimum conditions for function in response to internal and external changes.
A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland directly into the blood, which acts on target organs.
Gland that monitors and controls blood glucose concentration by releasing insulin and glucagon.
Hormone released by the pancreas when blood glucose is high; makes cells take up glucose and the liver convert glucose to glycogen.
Hormone released by the pancreas when blood glucose is low; causes the liver to convert glycogen to glucose.
Insoluble carbohydrate made of many glucose molecules, stored in the liver and muscles.
A change triggers a response that reverses the change, returning the condition to its normal level.
Hormones with opposite effects on the same condition, such as insulin and glucagon.
The organ with the specific receptors that responds to a particular hormone.
Condition in which the pancreas does not produce enough insulin.
Condition in which body cells no longer respond to insulin.
Reduced response of body cells to insulin, leading to high blood glucose.
Blood glucose concentration that is too low, e.g. after too much insulin.
A gland that secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream.
A diet that limits and spreads carbohydrate intake to avoid large rises in blood glucose.
A disease that cannot be passed from one person to another, such as diabetes.

worked.ans: Model answer: After the meal blood glucose concentration rises. The pancreas detects this and releases insulin into the blood. Insulin makes the liver and other cells take glucose out of the blood, and the liver converts glucose into glycogen, so the blood glucose concentration falls back to normal.
worked.q: Explain how the body brings blood glucose concentration back to normal after a meal containing a lot of carbohydrate. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: Blood glucose concentration rises and is detected by the pancreas.
Mark 2: The pancreas releases insulin into the blood.
Mark 3: Insulin makes cells (liver and muscle) take up glucose from the blood.
Mark 4: The liver converts glucose to glycogen for storage, so blood glucose falls to normal (negative feedback).

worked.ans: Model answer: In type 1 diabetes the pancreas cannot produce enough insulin, so insulin has to be injected. In type 2 diabetes insulin is made but the cells do not respond to it, so a controlled-carbohydrate diet, exercise and weight loss can improve the response and keep blood glucose normal.
worked.q: Explain why a person with type 1 diabetes is treated with insulin injections but a person with early type 2 diabetes may be treated with diet and exercise. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: In type 1 the pancreas does not produce enough insulin.
Mark 2: So insulin must be supplied by injection (it is a protein so is digested if swallowed).
Mark 3: In type 2 the body cells no longer respond to insulin.
Mark 4: Diet, exercise and weight loss improve the response of cells / reduce glucose intake, so injections may not be needed.
